work: Enarratio in Epistolam I B. Pauli ad Corinthios
source: Dionysii Cartusiani Opera Omnia, t. XIII (Montreuil)

1.title: Expositio capituli primi: Paulus vocatus apostolus, etc.
1.title_en: Explanation of the first chapter: Paul, called to be an apostle

paras.t: More solito, juxta consuetudinem scribendi epistolas seu litteras missivas, Apostolus in hujus epistolæ exordio nomen suum præmittit, et alterius secum scribentis, sicque procedit ad salutationem, narrationem et conclusionem, ut fieri solet. Et ait : Paulus vocatus, id est ex divina prædestinatione assumptus et factus, vel a Deo electus, apostolus Jesu Christi per voluntatem Dei, id est a voluntate divina, tanquam a causa principali ac libera. Hoc dicit Apostolus, ut ostendat eos Deo resistere, qui suo apostolatui contradicunt ; et etiam, ut demonstret quod ipse non injecit se ipsum, nec sibi assumpsit honorem, ut illi de quibus Dominus ait : Ego non mittebam eos, et ipsi currebant; et rursum, Principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi.
paras.en: As is usual, following the custom of writing epistles or letters, the Apostle at the opening of this epistle puts first his own name and that of another writing with him, and so goes on to the greeting, the narration and the conclusion, as is commonly done. And he says: [[1:1|Paul, called|Paulus vocatus]], that is, taken up and made by divine predestination, or chosen by God, [[1:1|to be an apostle of Jesus Christ by the will of God|apostolus Jesu Christi per voluntatem Dei]], that is, from the divine will, as from the principal and free cause. The Apostle says this to show that those who speak against his apostleship resist God; and also to show that he did not thrust himself in, [[Heb 5:4|Neither doth any man take the honour to himself|nec sibi assumpsit honorem]], like those of whom the Lord says: [[Jer 23:21|I did not send prophets, yet they ran|Ego non mittebam eos, et ipsi currebant]]; and again, [[Osee 8:4|they have been princes, and I knew not|Principes exstiterunt, et non cognovi]].

paras.t: Quæri potest, cur Paulus humillimus, in ista epistola, quum nomen suum commemorasset, statim adjecerit nomina eximiæ dignitatis, non solitæ humilitatis, dicens, Apostolus, non, Servus, Jesu Christi : et hoc, per voluntatem Dei, quasi impium […] sit aliter opinari. Et respondendum, quod virtus discretionis id exigit in prælato, ut ita se habeat verbis et factis circa subjectos, sicut eorum saluti expediens est. Oportet autem prælatum a subditis timeri, amari ac honorari. Quum ergo subjecti ita se habent circa prælatum, non est prælato necesse ut verbis seu factis auctoritatem suam ostendat. Quum vero contemnitur, ostendere debet collatæ potestatis auctoritatem, quatenus subditis timorem reverentiamque nominis sui incutiat. Apostolus autem Corinthiis viluit, quia ut asserit Glossa, contempto Paulo apostolo, de sapientibus hujus sæculi se jactitabant, quorum vana eloquentia sapientiaque terrena delectabantur. Idcirco Apostolus, ut eorum præsumptionem argueret, eos quoque ad suæ personæ reverentiam inclinaret, quum dixisset, Paulus, mox addidit, Apostolus, etc. Quod totum factum est, non ad propriam laudem, sed propter illorum salutem.
paras.en: It may be asked why Paul, most humble as he was, in this epistle, having mentioned his name, at once added names of outstanding dignity, not of his usual humility, saying "apostle," not "servant," of Jesus Christ: and this "by the will of God," as though it were wicked […] [a word is lost in the transcription] to think otherwise. The answer is that the virtue of discretion requires of a prelate that he behave in word and deed towards his subjects as is expedient for their salvation. A prelate must be feared, loved and honoured by his subjects. When, then, the subjects behave so towards the prelate, there is no need for him to show his authority in word or deed. But when he is despised, he must show the authority of the power conferred on him, so as to strike his subjects with fear and reverence for his name. Now the Apostle was held cheap by the Corinthians, because, as the Gloss asserts, despising Paul the apostle, they boasted of the wise men of this world, whose vain eloquence and earthly wisdom delighted them. So the Apostle, to rebuke their presumption and to bend them also to reverence for his person, having said "Paul," at once added "apostle," etc. All this was done not for his own praise, but for their salvation.

paras.t: Et Sosthenes frater. Hunc Sosthenem associat sibi Paulus, quia pro Corinthiorum correctione multum sollicitus fuit, et eos, ut dicitur, apud Apostolum accusavit. Unde nunc dicitur, Sosthenes frater, ad insinuandum quod accusatio illa prodiit ex fraterna caritate, non aliunde. Itaque, ego Paulus, et Sosthenes frater spiritualis, scribimus (solus tamen Paulus dictavit, Sosthenes vero consentiendo conscripsit) Ecclesiæ Dei, id est congregationi fidelium, quæ est Corinthi, id est in civitate Corinthia, utpote sanctificatis, id est a vitiis emundatis in sacramento Baptismi ac Pœnitentiæ, in Christo Jesu, id est in virtute et gratia Salvatoris, vocatis sanctis, id est a Deo ad sanctitatem adductis atque electis, cum omnibus qui invocant, id est, ex intimo cordis affectu implorant, nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi, in omni loco ipsorum, id est ubicumque in provincia Corinthiorum, et nostro, id est loco nobis primum concesso. Hic enim locus Paulo commissus est, ut habitatores ejus converteret. Et quum Deus ubique sit, non solum in templo materiali, sed ubique invocandus est, quatenus veri adoratores adorent eum in spiritu et veritate : quia nec contemplatio, neque oratio exigit locum, aut loci determinationem ex necessitate, sed ex quadam decentia. Unde sicut contemplationi Beatorum deputatur cœlum empyreum ex congruentia, sic ecclesia materialis deputatur orationi fidelium ex congruentia quadam. Sed sicut angelus ubicumque fuerit extra cœlum empyreum, incessabiliter Deum contemplatur ; ita fidelis ubicumque fuerit, nomen Christi invocare debet. Et sumitur hic nomen pro re nominata.
paras.en: [[1:1|and Sosthenes a brother|Et Sosthenes frater]]. Paul joins this Sosthenes to himself because he was very anxious for the correction of the Corinthians, and, as is said, accused them before the Apostle. So it now says "Sosthenes a brother," to hint that that accusation came from brotherly charity and from nothing else. So: I Paul, and Sosthenes my spiritual brother, write (though Paul alone dictated, and Sosthenes wrote with him by consenting) [[1:2|To the church of God|Ecclesiæ Dei]], that is, to the congregation of the faithful, [[1:2|that is at Corinth|quæ est Corinthi]], that is, in the city of Corinth, namely [[1:2|to them that are sanctified|sanctificatis]], that is, cleansed of vices in the sacrament of Baptism and of Penance, [[1:2|in Christ Jesus|in Christo Jesu]], that is, in the power and grace of the Saviour, [[1:2|called to be saints|vocatis sanctis]], that is, brought and chosen by God to holiness, [[1:2|with all that invoke|cum omnibus qui invocant]], that is, implore from the inmost affection of the heart, [[1:2|the name of our Lord Jesus Christ in every place of theirs|nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi, in omni loco ipsorum]], that is, wherever in the province of the Corinthians, [[1:2|and ours|et nostro]], that is, the place first granted to us. For this place was committed to Paul, that he might convert its inhabitants. And since God is everywhere, He is to be called upon not only in the material temple but everywhere, so that [[John 4:23|the true adorers shall adore the Father in spirit and in truth|veri adoratores adorent eum in spiritu et veritate]]: for neither contemplation nor prayer requires a place, or a set place, of necessity, but out of a certain fittingness. So, just as the empyrean heaven is assigned by fittingness to the contemplation of the Blessed, so the material church is assigned by a certain fittingness to the prayer of the faithful. But just as an angel, wherever he is outside the empyrean heaven, contemplates God without ceasing, so the faithful man, wherever he is, should call upon the name of Christ. And "name" is taken here for the thing named.

paras.t: Consequenter salutatio ponitur : Gratia gratum faciens (de qua in expositione primi capituli epistolæ ad Romanos dictum est plenius) detur et semper insit vobis Corinthiis, et pax, id est quies mentis a vitiorum inordinato impulsu, a Deo Patre nostro per gratiam adoptionis, qui est Pater Christi per realem relationem ac relativam proprietatem, et Pater Christi per æternam ac naturalem generationem, et a Domino Jesu Christo Filio Patris, qui secundum divinam naturam est una et eadem causa efficiens gratiæ et pacis cum Patre. Quæcumque enim facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit. Secundum naturam vero assumptam, est causa gratiæ et ceterorum donorum gratuitorum instrumentalis ac meritoria. Patre autem et Filio nominatis, datur intelligi Spiritus Sanctus, qui est amor, nexus et germen amborum. Totius superfelicissimæ Trinitatis indivisa est operatio foris transiens, sicut et trium Personarum est una natura et una potestas.
paras.en: Next comes the greeting: [[1:3|Grace|Gratia]], sanctifying grace [*gratia gratum faciens*, the grace that makes one pleasing to God] (of which more was said in the explanation of the first chapter of the epistle to the Romans), be given and ever be [[1:3|to you|vobis]] Corinthians, [[1:3|and peace|et pax]], that is, rest of mind from the disordered drive of the vices, [[1:3|from God our father|a Deo Patre nostro]] by the grace of adoption, who is the Father of Christ [the transcription reads "Christi" here; the sense requires "our Father"] by a real relation and a relative property, and the Father of Christ by eternal and natural generation, [[1:3|and from the Lord Jesus Christ|et a Domino Jesu Christo]], the Son of the Father, who according to the divine nature is one and the same efficient cause of grace and peace with the Father. For [[John 5:19|what things soever he doth, these the Son also doth in like manner|Quæcumque enim facit Pater, hæc et Filius similiter facit]]. According to the nature He assumed, He is the instrumental and meritorious cause of grace and of the other gratuitous gifts. The Father and the Son being named, the Holy Ghost is understood, who is the love, bond and offspring of both. The outward working of the whole most blessed Trinity is undivided, as the three Persons have one nature and one power.

paras.t: Quoniam vero inter Corinthios erant aliqui boni laude digni, Apostolus primo agit de bonis, et pro beneficiis Dei eis collatis gratias agit, et ait : Gratias ago verbis, factis, atque affectibus, Deo meo : qui licet sit omnium Deus, tanto tamen specialius ac singularius est Deus uniuscujusque ipsum colentis, quanto ab eo devotius colitur ardentiusque amatur. Unde et princeps theologorum Dionysius, in libris suis vix dicere audens, Deus meus, sic dicit : Deus, et si fas est dicere, meus. Propterea non quorumlibet, sed perfectorum ferventer amantium est dicere, Deus meus. Fortiter tamen proficientes, ex quadam humili confidentia dicere possunt, Deus meus ; alii passim non dicant, Deus meus, nisi in persona Christi hominis, vel Ecclesiæ seu perfectorum. Itaque, Gratias ago Deo meo, a cujus amore nulla creatura me potest avellere, semper, id est omni hora convenienti ac debita : juxta quem modum jubemur semper orare ; pro vobis, quorum imperfectum supplere desidero, eo quod diligam vos tanquam me ipsum, in gratia Dei quæ data est vobis, id est pro omnibus donis supernaturalibus, vobis divinitus condonatis, in Christo Jesu, id est per Christum mediatorem, seu merito ejus, per quem omnia dona divina nobis præstantur.
paras.en: Since among the Corinthians there were some good men worthy of praise, the Apostle deals first with the good, and gives thanks for the benefits of God bestowed on them, and says: [[1:4|I give thanks|Gratias ago]] in words, deeds and affections [[1:4|to my God|Deo meo]]: who, though He is the God of all, is yet the more especially and singularly the God of each one who worships Him, the more devoutly He is worshipped and the more ardently He is loved by him. So Dionysius too, the prince of theologians, hardly daring in his books to say "my God," says thus: "God, and if it is lawful to say so, mine." For this reason it belongs not to anyone at all, but to the perfect who love fervently, to say "my God." Yet those who are making strong progress can say "my God" out of a certain humble confidence; let others not say "my God" commonly, except in the person of Christ as man, or of the Church or of the perfect. So: I give thanks to my God, from whose love no creature can tear me away[[Rom 8:38||]][[Rom 8:39||]], [[1:4|always|semper]], that is, at every fitting and due hour: in the way in which we are commanded [[Luke 18:1|always to pray|semper orare]]; [[1:4|for you|pro vobis]], whose shortcomings I desire to make up, because I love you as myself, [[1:4|for the grace of God that is given you|in gratia Dei quæ data est vobis]], that is, for all the supernatural gifts granted you by God, [[1:4|in Christ Jesus|in Christo Jesu]], that is, through Christ the mediator, or by His merit, through whom all divine gifts are given us.

paras.t: Quia in omnibus spiritualibus divitiis divites facti estis in illo, id est, per Christum abundatis in omni gratia Dei, secundum conditionem et statum hujus fragilis vitæ, videlicet, quia in his quæ ad salutem requiruntur, abundatis. Secundum quem sensum ait Psalmista : Nihil deest timentibus eum. Vel ideo dicuntur in omnibus divites facti, quoniam spiritualia bona quæ nondum sortiti sunt in re, jam habent in spe. Has autem divitias explicat Apostolus in speciali. In omni verbo evangelicæ prædicationis. Hoc dicit Apostolus, vel quia donum linguarum receperunt, ita ut omnibus linguis loquerentur. In primitiva enim Ecclesia, per impositionem manuum Apostolorum dabatur baptizatis donum linguarum. Vel, In omni verbo, id est in omni modo docendi. Et in omni scientia vera ad salutem necessaria, videlicet in intellectu Scripturarum sanctarum. Sicut testimonium Christi confirmatum est in vobis : id est, eo modo divites facti estis in his, sicut, id est prout, testimonium Christi confirmatum est in vobis, id est, promissio seu contestatio qua Christus testatus est se ditaturum suos fideles, in vobis impleta est. Ipse enim prædixit : Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ. Hoc autem dixit de Spiritu, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum. Et alibi : Quidquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, hoc faciam. Ita ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gratia necessaria ad salutem ; vel, quia omnia dona ad gratiam gratum facientem pertinentia habetis, et in aliis gratiis, scilicet gratis datis, notabiliter abundatis. Virtutes enim et dona Spiritus Sancti ita connexa sunt, ut habens unum, cetera quoque aliqualiter habeat. Non tamen ita perfecti fuerunt, quin potuerunt proficere perfectioresque fieri, juxta illud : Omnem qui fert fructum, purgabit eum Pater, ut fructum plus afferat.
paras.en: [[1:5|That in all things you are made rich in him|Quia in omnibus spiritualibus divitiis divites facti estis in illo]]: in all spiritual riches, that is, through Christ you abound in all the grace of God, according to the condition and state of this frail life, namely, because you abound in what is required for salvation. In this sense the Psalmist says: [[Ps 33:10|there is no want to them that fear him|Nihil deest timentibus eum]]. Or they are said to have been made rich in all things because the spiritual goods which they have not yet obtained in fact, they already have in hope. The Apostle sets out these riches in particular. [[1:5|in all utterance|In omni verbo]] of the preaching of the Gospel. The Apostle says this either because they had received the gift of tongues, so that they spoke in all tongues: for in the early Church the gift of tongues was given to the baptized by the laying on of the Apostles' hands[[Acts 19:6||]]. Or, in all utterance, that is, in every way of teaching. [[1:5|and in all knowledge|Et in omni scientia]], true knowledge necessary for salvation, namely in the understanding of the holy Scriptures. [[1:6|As the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you|Sicut testimonium Christi confirmatum est in vobis]]: that is, you have been made rich in these things in such a way as, that is, according as, the testimony of Christ was confirmed in you, that is, the promise or witness by which Christ testified that He would enrich His faithful has been fulfilled in you. For He foretold: [[John 7:38|He that believeth in me, as the scripture saith: Out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water|Qui credit in me, flumina de ventre ejus fluent aquæ vivæ]]. [[John 7:39|Now this he said of the Spirit which they should receive who believed in him|Hoc autem dixit de Spiritu, quem accepturi erant credentes in eum]]. And elsewhere: [[John 14:13|whatsoever you shall ask the Father in my name, that will I do|Quidquid petieritis Patrem in nomine meo, hoc faciam]]. [[1:7|So that nothing is wanting to you in any grace|Ita ut nihil vobis desit in ulla gratia]] necessary for salvation; or, because you have all the gifts belonging to sanctifying grace, and abound notably in the other graces too, namely those freely given. For the virtues and gifts of the Holy Ghost are so linked that one who has one has the others too in some measure. Yet they were not so perfect that they could not make progress and become more perfect, according to the words: [[John 15:2|every one that beareth fruit, he will purge it, that it may bring forth more fruit|Omnem qui fert fructum, purgabit eum Pater, ut fructum plus afferat]].

paras.t: Itaque, nihil gratiæ deest vobis exspectantibus revelationem, id est manifestam apparitionem, Domini nostri Jesu Christi in die judicii, quando juxta Isaiam prophetam, videbit omnis caro Salutare Dei nostri. De qua revelatione scriptum est : Ecce venit cum nubibus, et videbit eum omnis oculus, et qui eum pupugerunt. Vel, Revelationem Christi, id est claram visionem ejus in patria : quæ visio est tota merces. De qua ait in Evangelio : Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo ; et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum. Qui et confirmabit vos, ut pie confido (verbum est bonæ spei, non absolutæ assertionis, nisi forte ex revelatione divina), usque in finem vitæ præsentis inclusive, sine crimine, id est mortali peccato, ita quod gratiam perseverantiæ conferet vobis, ne peccetis mortaliter, sed in gratia decedatis : ad hoc, ut sine peccato appareatis in die adventus Domini nostri Jesu Christi, id est in die judicii. Vel, adventus Christi, intelligitur spiritualis ejus adventus, quo quotidie venit per gratiam ad electos (prout ipse Christus profitetur : Ad eum veniemus et mansionem apud eum faciemus ; et alibi, Ego sto ad ostium et pulso) ; vel, visitatio ejus qua visitat unumquemque in morte. Unde ait : Vigilate, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit. De hoc adventu comminatur quodam loco cuique negligenti : Si non vigilaveris, veniam ad te tanquam fur, et nescies qua hora veniam. Sed et Jacobus dicit : Patientes estote usque ad adventum Domini, id est usque ad mortem. Unde subjungitur ibidem : Ecce judex ante januam adsistit. Quandocumque autem confirmamur a Deo, Christus spiritualiter venit ad nos.
paras.en: So no grace is wanting to you, [[1:7|waiting for the manifestation of our Lord Jesus Christ|exspectantibus revelationem Domini nostri Jesu Christi]], the manifestation, that is, the open appearing, of our Lord Jesus Christ on the day of judgment, when, according to the prophet Isaias, [[Is 40:5|all flesh together shall see|videbit omnis caro]] the salvation of our God [the margin gives Is. xi, 5; the words are those of Is 40:5 as quoted in Luke 3:6]. Of this manifestation it is written: [[Apoc 1:7|Behold, he cometh with the clouds, and every eye shall see him: and they also that pierced him|Ecce venit cum nubibus, et videbit eum omnis oculus, et qui eum pupugerunt]]. Or, the manifestation of Christ, that is, the clear vision of Him in the fatherland, which vision is the whole reward. Of it He says in the Gospel: [[John 14:21|he that loveth me shall be loved of my Father: and I will love him and will manifest myself to him|Qui diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo ; et ego diligam eum, et manifestabo ei me ipsum]]. [[1:8|Who also will confirm you|Qui et confirmabit vos]], as I piously trust (it is a word of good hope, not of absolute assertion, unless perhaps from divine revelation), [[1:8|unto the end|usque in finem]] of the present life, inclusively, [[1:8|without crime|sine crimine]], that is, mortal sin, so that He will confer on you the grace of perseverance, that you may not sin mortally but die in grace: to this end, that you may appear without sin [[1:8|in the days of the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ|in die adventus Domini nostri Jesu Christi]], that is, on the day of judgment. Or, by the coming of Christ is understood His spiritual coming, by which He comes daily by grace to the elect (as Christ Himself declares: [[John 14:23|we will come to him and will make our abode with him|Ad eum veniemus et mansionem apud eum faciemus]]; and elsewhere, [[Apoc 3:20|Behold, I stand at the gate and knock|Ego sto ad ostium et pulso]]); or His visitation, by which He visits each one at death. So He says: [[Matt 24:42|Watch ye therefore, because you know not what hour your Lord will come|Vigilate, quia nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit]]. Of this coming He threatens every negligent man in a certain place: [[Apoc 3:3|If then thou shalt not watch, I will come to thee as a thief: and thou shalt not know at what hour I will come to thee|Si non vigilaveris, veniam ad te tanquam fur, et nescies qua hora veniam]]. And James too says: [[Jas 5:7|Be patient therefore, brethren, until the coming of the Lord|Patientes estote usque ad adventum Domini]], that is, until death. So it is added in the same place: [[Jas 5:9|Behold the judge standeth before the door|Ecce judex ante januam adsistit]]. Whenever we are confirmed by God, Christ comes to us spiritually.

paras.t: Fidelis Deus, non a fide, sed a fidelitate quam conservat ad suos, cum quibus fideliter agit, secundum quod caritas dictat. Vel, Fidelis Deus, id est verax in promissis, juxta illud in Psalmo : Fidelis Dominus in omnibus verbis suis. Per quem, id est a quo, vocati estis per inspirationem internam ac prædicationem apostolicam, in societatem, id est ad communionem et participationem gratiæ et gloriæ Filii ejus Jesu Christi Domini nostri. De plenitudine siquidem ejus accepimus omnes. Prædestinavit enim nos conformes fieri imaginis Filii sui, ut alio loco dictum est. Ecce quanta gratia et benevolentia Dei sancti et benedicti, qui non solum vocavit nos ad consortium Apostolorum et angelorum, sed unigeniti Filii sui. Quotquot enim receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri. Ideo scriptum est : Maxima et pretiosa nobis promissa donavit, ut per hæc efficiamini divinæ consortes naturæ; et alibi, Societas nostra sit cum Patre et Filio ejus Jesu Christo. Ineffabilis prorsus nobilitas, societatem habere cum Deo; et summa miseria, propter temporales delicias ac transitoria bona vilissima atque caduca, societatem hanc deiformem amittere. Non ergo negligamus gratiam Dei quæ data est nobis; sed carnem domemus, affectum purgemus, cœlestibus infatigabiliter intendamus.
paras.en: [[1:9|God is faithful|Fidelis Deus]], not from faith, but from the faithfulness He keeps towards His own, with whom He deals faithfully, as charity dictates. Or, God is faithful, that is, true in His promises, according to the words in the Psalm: [[Ps 144:13|The Lord is faithful in all his words|Fidelis Dominus in omnibus verbis suis]]. [[1:9|by whom|Per quem]], that is, from whom, [[1:9|you are called|vocati estis]] by inward inspiration and apostolic preaching, [[1:9|unto the fellowship|in societatem]], that is, to the communion and sharing of the grace and glory [[1:9|of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord|Filii ejus Jesu Christi Domini nostri]]. For [[John 1:16|of his fulness we all have received|De plenitudine siquidem ejus accepimus omnes]]. For He [[Rom 8:29|predestinated to be made conformable to the image of his Son|Prædestinavit enim nos conformes fieri imaginis Filii sui]], as was said in another place. See how great is the grace and goodwill of the holy and blessed God, who has called us not only to the company of the Apostles and angels, but of His only-begotten Son. For [[John 1:12|as many as received him, he gave them power to be made the sons of God|Quotquot enim receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri]]. So it is written: [[2 Pet 1:4|he hath given us most great and precious promises: that by these you may be made partakers of the divine nature|Maxima et pretiosa nobis promissa donavit, ut per hæc efficiamini divinæ consortes naturæ]]; and elsewhere, [[1 John 1:3|our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ|Societas nostra sit cum Patre et Filio ejus Jesu Christo]]. An altogether unspeakable nobility, to have fellowship with God; and the greatest misery, to lose this godlike fellowship for the sake of temporal delights and passing goods, most worthless and perishing. Let us not, then, [[1 Tim 4:14|Neglect not the grace|negligamus gratiam]] of God which has been given us; but let us tame the flesh, purify our affection, and tend tirelessly to heavenly things.

paras.t: Hucusque laudavit Apostolus perfectos; jam alios hortatur ad perfectionem illorum. Obsecro autem, id est, per rem sacram, imo per Sanctum Sanctorum rogo, vos, fratres, videlicet per nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi : ut id ipsum, id est unum et idem secundum Dei voluntatem, dicatis omnes, sicut faciunt quos jam laudavi, et non sint in vobis schismata, id est divisiones atque discordiæ. Scriptum enim est : Divisum est cor eorum, nunc interibunt. Sed videtur contrarium his, quod Dominus ait per alium Prophetam : Scindite corda vestra, et non vestimenta vestra. Et respondendum, quod loquitur de spirituali cordis circumcisione et apertione, qua cor antea durum aperitur verbo Dei, et recipit illud. Sitis autem perfecti, id est perfecte seu omnino concordes, in eodem sensu, id est in cognitione practica, ut idem agatis, et in eadem scientia, id est in cognitione speculativa, ut idem credatis ac sapiatis. Duæ enim sunt partes legis divinæ, videlicet testimonia, et præcepta. Testimonia pertinent ad credenda, præcepta vero ad operanda. Vult ergo Apostolus, ut in horum utroque conformes sint.
paras.en: So far the Apostle has praised the perfect; now he exhorts the others to their perfection. [[1:10|Now I beseech you, brethren|Obsecro autem vos fratres]], that is, I ask by a sacred thing, indeed by the Holy of Holies, namely [[1:10|by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ|per nomen Domini nostri Jesu Christi]]: [[1:10|that you all speak the same thing|ut id ipsum, id est unum et idem secundum Dei voluntatem, dicatis omnes]], the same thing, that is, one and the same according to the will of God, as those do whom I have just praised, [[1:10|and that there be no schisms among you|et non sint in vobis schismata]], that is, divisions and discords. For it is written: [[Osee 10:2|Their heart is divided: now they shall perish|Divisum est cor eorum, nunc interibunt]]. But what the Lord says through another Prophet seems contrary to this: [[Joel 2:13|rend your hearts, and not your garments|Scindite corda vestra, et non vestimenta vestra]]. The answer is that he speaks of the spiritual circumcision and opening of the heart, by which a heart that was hard before is opened by the word of God and receives it. [[1:10|but that you be perfect|Sitis autem perfecti]], that is, perfectly or wholly of one accord, [[1:10|in the same mind|in eodem sensu]], that is, in practical knowledge, so that you do the same, [[1:10|and in the same judgment|et in eadem scientia]], that is, in speculative knowledge, so that you believe and understand the same [Denis's text reads *scientia*, "knowledge", where the Vulgate has *sententia*]. For there are two parts of the divine law, namely the testimonies and the precepts. The testimonies concern what is to be believed, the precepts what is to be done. The Apostle wants them, then, to be conformed in both.

paras.t: Hæc hortor et obsecro : Significatum est enim mihi de vobis, o fratres mei, ab his qui sunt Chloes, id est, qui habitant in loco qui dicitur Chloes, vel in domo religiosæ feminæ Chloes vocatæ : quorum unus fuerat Sosthenes, jam prædictus. Secundum quosdam, Chloes est nomen loci prope Corinthum ; secundum alios vero, est nomen mulieris devotæ in cujus domo multi fideles manebant. Isti doluerunt de contentione ac schismate Corinthiorum, dixeruntque Paulo quod subditur : quia contentiones sunt inter vos : sicut subjungitur. Hoc autem dico, id est refero, quod unusquisque vestrum dicit. Percepi enim verba vestra in propria forma, et ideo omnium vestrum verba jam enarro. Alius enim e vobis dicit : Ego quidem sum Pauli, id est, ad Paulum pertineo tanquam filius et discipulus ejus, quia ab eo baptizatus seu doctus sum. Alius dicit : Ego autem sum Apollo, id est discipulus ejus. Iste est Apollo, vir eloquens et potens in Scripturis, sicut in Actibus legitur : qui ut dicitur, erat Corinthiorum episcopus. Alius dicit : Ego vero Cephæ, id est, ego ad Petrum pertineo. Alius dicit : Ego autem Christi sum, tanquam ejus servus atque discipulus. Qui ita dixerunt, non erraverunt ut alii. Contentio autem Corinthiorum fuit ex hoc, quod putabant sacramentum Baptismatis aliquid virtutis habere ex meritis ministri, et ita baptizatus ab uno, prætulit se baptizato ab alio, prout unus ministrorum excellentior exstitit alio. Quilibet etiam nominavit se ab illo a quo fuerat baptizatus : sicque unus dicebat, Ego sum Pauli.
paras.en: I urge and beseech these things: [[1:11|For it hath been signified unto me, my brethren, of you|Significatum est enim mihi de vobis, o fratres mei]], [[1:11|by them that are of the house of Chloe|ab his qui sunt Chloes]], that is, who live in the place called Chloe, or in the house of a devout woman named Chloe: one of whom was Sosthenes, already mentioned. According to some, Chloe is the name of a place near Corinth; according to others, it is the name of a devout woman in whose house many of the faithful lived. These grieved over the contention and schism of the Corinthians, and told Paul what follows: [[1:11|that there are contentions among you|quia contentiones sunt inter vos]], as is added. [[1:12|Now this I say, that every one of you saith|Hoc autem dico, quod unusquisque vestrum dicit]]: I say, that is, I report. For I have heard your words in their own form, and so I now tell the words of all of you. For one of you says: [[1:12|I indeed am of Paul|Ego quidem sum Pauli]], that is, I belong to Paul as his son and disciple, because I was baptized or taught by him. Another says: [[1:12|and I am of Apollo|Ego autem sum Apollo]], that is, his disciple. This is Apollo, an eloquent man and mighty in the Scriptures, as we read in the Acts[[Acts 18:24||]]: who, as is said, was bishop of the Corinthians. Another says: [[1:12|and I of Cephas|Ego vero Cephæ]], that is, I belong to Peter. Another says: [[1:12|and I of Christ|Ego autem Christi sum]], as His servant and disciple. Those who spoke so did not err as the others did. The contention of the Corinthians came from this, that they thought the sacrament of Baptism had some power from the merits of the minister, and so one baptized by one man preferred himself to one baptized by another, according as one of the ministers was more excellent than the other. Each also named himself after the one by whom he had been baptized: and so one said, I am of Paul.

paras.t: Hi erraverunt, quia Baptismus non habet efficaciam nisi merito Christi tanquam a causa meritoria, qui tactu suæ mundissimæ carnis, vim regenerativam contulit aquis. Unde de latere Christi morientis dicuntur omnia sacramenta fluxisse, quoniam virtute passionis dominicæ operantur. Christus vero ut Deus, seu tota beatissima Trinitas, est causa effectiva et principalis virtutis Baptismi, quoniam solus Deus intus baptizat, peccata lavando seu abluendo, et gratiam infundendo, sine cujus infusione nemo justificatur, neque peccatum dimittitur. Unde quodam loco de Christo habetur : Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem et manentem super eum, ipse est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto. Et alibi ait idem Joannes Baptista : Ipse baptizabit vos Spiritu Sancto et igni. Unde ut legitur, ad vitandum prædictum Corinthiorum errorem, Ecclesia Græcorum mutavit formam Baptismi, dicendo : Baptizetur servus Jesu Christi.
paras.en: These erred, because Baptism has no efficacy except by the merit of Christ as its meritorious cause, who by the touch of His most pure flesh gave regenerating power to the waters. So all the sacraments are said to have flowed from the side of the dying Christ, since they work by the power of the Lord's passion. But Christ as God, or the whole most blessed Trinity, is the efficient and principal cause of the power of Baptism, since God alone baptizes inwardly, washing or cleansing sins away and pouring in grace, without the infusion of which no one is justified and no sin is forgiven. So it is said of Christ in one place: [[John 1:33|He upon whom thou shalt see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he it is that baptizeth with the Holy Ghost|Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem et manentem super eum, ipse est qui baptizat in Spiritu Sancto]]. And elsewhere the same John the Baptist says: [[Matt 3:11|he shall baptize you in the Holy Ghost and fire|Ipse baptizabit vos Spiritu Sancto et igni]]. So, as we read, to avoid this error of the Corinthians the Church of the Greeks changed the form of Baptism, saying: "Let the servant of Jesus Christ be baptized."

paras.t: Ad ostendendum ergo errorem Corinthiorum, quærit Apostolus : Divisus est Christus ? id est, numquid Christus in corpore suo mystico hujuscemodi divisionem admittit et approbat, ut unus dicatur Pauli, alius Cephæ, et non potius omnes sint Christi, et ab ipso Christiani vocentur? Quasi dicat, Non. Christus enim ait : Pater sancte, serva eos in nomine tuo, quos dedisti mihi, ut sint unum, sicut et nos. Vel sic : Divisus est Christus ? id est, numquid Christus diversimode se habet ad suos ministros baptistas, aliter operando in Baptismo unius quam alterius ? Numquid Paulus crucifixus est pro vobis, aut in nomine Pauli baptizati estis ? id est, quum nec Paulus nec aliquis alius, præter Christum, pro vestra salute sit passus, nec in nomine Pauli vel alterius, sed in nomine Christi baptizati sitis, constat quod non plus valet Baptismus ministratus ab uno ministro Christi quam ab alio : quoniam virtus Baptismi, est ab ipso qui pro mundi salute occisus est, et in cujus nomine administratur : hic vero Christus est. Quamvis autem Christus dixerit, Euntes, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti, Apostoli tamen in primitiva Ecclesia, ex familiari consilio seu instinctu Spiritus Sancti, videlicet ut nomen Christi magis celebre fieret, quod a Judæis jugiter blasphemabatur, baptizaverunt in nomine Christi. Unde Petrus disseruit : Baptizetur, inquiens, unusquisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi. Hoc tamen fecerunt, secundum quod in nomine Christi, tota supersancta Trinitas intelligitur, videlicet Pater ungens, et Spiritus Sanctus, qui est unctio.
paras.en: To show the error of the Corinthians, then, the Apostle asks: [[1:13|Is Christ divided|Divisus est Christus]]? that is, does Christ admit and approve such a division in His mystical body, that one be called Paul's, another Cephas's, and not rather that all be Christ's and be called Christians from Him? As if he said: No. For Christ says: [[John 17:11|Holy Father, keep them in thy name whom thou hast given me: that they may be one, as we also are|Pater sancte, serva eos in nomine tuo, quos dedisti mihi, ut sint unum, sicut et nos]]. Or thus: Is Christ divided? that is, does Christ stand in different ways towards His ministers who baptize, working otherwise in the Baptism of one than of another? [[1:13|Was Paul then crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul|Numquid Paulus crucifixus est pro vobis, aut in nomine Pauli baptizati estis]]? That is, since neither Paul nor anyone else but Christ suffered for your salvation, and you were baptized not in the name of Paul or another but in the name of Christ, it is plain that Baptism given by one minister of Christ is worth no more than by another: since the power of Baptism is from Him who was slain for the salvation of the world, and in whose name it is administered: and this is Christ. Although Christ said, [[Matt 28:19|Going therefore, teach ye all nations: baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Ghost|Euntes, docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos in nomine Patris et Filii et Spiritus Sancti]], yet the Apostles in the early Church, by intimate counsel or prompting of the Holy Ghost, namely that the name of Christ, which was constantly blasphemed by the Jews, might become more renowned, baptized in the name of Christ. So Peter declared: [[Acts 2:38|be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ|Baptizetur, inquiens, unusquisque vestrum in nomine Jesu Christi]]. Yet they did this in so far as in the name of Christ the whole most holy Trinity is understood, namely the Father who anoints and the Holy Ghost who is the anointing.

paras.t: Gratias ago Deo meo, quod neminem vestrum baptizavi nisi Crispum et Caium. Iste videtur esse Crispus archisynagogus, qui, ut in Actibus legitur, credidit Domino. Caius quoque iste forsitan est, de quo ad Romanos dixit Apostolus, Salutat vos Caius hospes meus : cui, ut ibidem dictum est, Joannes tertiam suam misit epistolam; eratque Corinthiorum episcopus. Itaque, Gratias ago, quod neminem vestrum baptizavi præter hos paucos : qui etiam non sunt de vestra contentione, quum sint viri perfecti : non quia baptizare sit actus malus, sed ne quis dicat, quod in nomine meo baptizati sitis, id est, ne actus bonus a me factus, esset vobis occasio mali. Ex quo elucescit, quod interdum ab aliquibus bonis operibus ex caritate cessandum sit, ut aliorum culpa seu scandalum devitetur. Baptizavi autem et Stephanæ domum, id est illius devotæ matronæ familiam, forte simul cum ea : quæ etiam non contendit vobiscum. Ceterum nescio si quem alium vestrum baptizavi. Et quia Apostolus bonæ memoriæ erat, probabile est quod non baptizavit nisi prædictos tam paucos. Cujus ratio subditur.
paras.en: [[1:14|I give God thanks, that I baptized none of you but Crispus and Caius|Gratias ago Deo meo, quod neminem vestrum baptizavi nisi Crispum et Caium]]. This seems to be Crispus the ruler of the synagogue, who, as we read in the Acts, believed in the Lord[[Acts 18:8||]]. This Caius is perhaps the one of whom the Apostle said to the Romans, [[Rom 16:23|Caius, my host, and the whole church saluteth you|Salutat vos Caius hospes meus]]: to whom, as was said there, John sent his third epistle; and he was bishop of the Corinthians. So: I give thanks that I baptized none of you except these few, who are also not of your contention, since they are perfect men: not because baptizing is a bad act, but [[1:15|Lest any should say that you were baptized in my name|ne quis dicat, quod in nomine meo baptizati sitis]], that is, lest a good act done by me should be an occasion of evil to you. From this it is clear that sometimes one must out of charity stop doing certain good works, so that the fault or scandal of others may be avoided. [[1:16|And I baptized also the household of Stephanus|Baptizavi autem et Stephanæ domum]], that is, the household of that devout matron [so Denis takes Stephanas], perhaps together with her: who also does not contend with you. [[1:16|Besides, I know not whether I baptized any other|Ceterum nescio si quem alium vestrum baptizavi]]. And since the Apostle had a good memory, it is likely that he baptized none but these few. The reason for this is added.

paras.t: Non enim misit me Christus baptizare, id est principaliter ad baptizandum, quum hoc ab inferioribus et parum doctis fieri possit tam perfecte sicut a perfectioribus, sed evangelizare, id est Evangelium prædicare : quod non potuit perfecte fieri nisi a valde perfectis atque doctissimis. Non tamen est sic intelligendum quod nunc dixit Apostolus, Non misit me Christus baptizare, quasi ipse et alii Apostoli nequaquam missi sint baptizare, quum dicat eis Salvator, Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos : sed hoc ideo dicitur, quia Apostoli non sunt principaliter missi ad baptizandum, videlicet ne baptizando retardarentur a prædicatione. Ideoque, quemadmodum Christus per se ipsum docuit, et per discipulos baptizavit, ut patet apud Joannem; sic et Apostoli verbo prædicationis instabant, et per discipulos suos frequentius baptizabant, interdum vero per se, necessitate aut magna ratione exigente baptizationis. Itaque, Misit me Christus evangelizare, non in sapientia verbi, id est non in sapientia naturali, seu philosophica, verbis ornata atque verbosa, quæ comparatione divinæ sapientiæ potius est sapientia nominalis, quam realis, ut non evacuetur, id est, incredibilis aut inutilis reputetur, crux Christi, id est fides passionis dominicæ. Naturali enim rationi visum est impossibile, incredibile atque inutile, ut Deus pateretur: ideo Apostolus fidem crucis Christi non prædicavit in sapientia verbi. Vel sic: Ut non evacuetur crux Christi, id est, ne fides Christi videatur humanæ rationi inniti, et per consequens, faciliter posse reprobari. Denique christiana doctrina non indiget cultu et pompa verborum, ne videatur ex humanæ subtilitatis calliditate procedere, non ex veritate. Ibi enim compositio sermonis exquiritur, ubi ipsa se veritas non commendat.
paras.en: [[1:17|For Christ sent me not to baptize|Non enim misit me Christus baptizare]], that is, principally to baptize, since this can be done by lesser and little-learned men as perfectly as by the more perfect, [[1:17|but to preach the gospel|sed evangelizare]]: which could not be done perfectly except by the very perfect and most learned. Yet what the Apostle has just said, "Christ sent me not to baptize," is not to be understood as if he and the other Apostles were not sent to baptize at all, since the Saviour says to them, [[Matt 28:19|teach ye all nations: baptizing them|Docete omnes gentes, baptizantes eos]]; but it is said because the Apostles were not sent principally to baptize, namely lest they be held back from preaching by baptizing. And so, just as Christ taught by Himself and baptized through His disciples, as is plain in John[[John 4:2||]], so the Apostles too pressed on with the word of preaching, and baptized more often through their disciples, but sometimes by themselves, when need or great reason called for baptizing. So: Christ sent me to preach the gospel, [[1:17|not in wisdom of speech|non in sapientia verbi]], that is, not in natural or philosophical wisdom, adorned with words and wordy, which compared with divine wisdom is a wisdom in name rather than in fact, [[1:17|lest the cross of Christ should be made void|Ut non evacuetur crux Christi]], made void, that is, held incredible or useless; the cross of Christ, that is, faith in the Lord's passion. For to natural reason it seemed impossible, incredible and useless that God should suffer: so the Apostle did not preach the faith of Christ's cross in wisdom of speech. Or thus: lest the cross of Christ be made void, that is, lest the faith of Christ seem to rest on human reason, and so be easily refuted. Moreover Christian teaching does not need the ornament and pomp of words, lest it seem to come from the cunning of human subtlety and not from the truth. For a careful arrangement of speech is sought where the truth does not commend itself.

paras.t: Verbum enim, id est fides et prædicatio, crucis Christi, pereuntibus quidem, id est mundi hujus sapientibus et reprobis, stultitia est, id est, stulta et irridenda videtur: sicut de Græcis refert Dionysius, quod audita prædicatione fidei christianæ, lato ore riserunt. His autem qui salvi fiunt, id est nobis, puta electis, virtus Dei est, id est potens effectus divinæ potentiæ, per quem obtinemus gratiam et gloriam, victoriam quoque contra insidias hostis, juxta illud: Hæc est victoria quæ vincit mundum, fides nostra: quis enim est qui vincit mundum, nisi qui credit quoniam Jesus est Filius Dei?
paras.en: [[1:18|For the word of the cross|Verbum enim crucis]], that is, the faith and preaching of Christ's cross, [[1:18|to them indeed that perish|pereuntibus quidem]], that is, to the wise of this world and the reprobate, [[1:18|is foolishness|stultitia est]], that is, seems foolish and laughable: as Dionysius relates of the Greeks, that when they heard the preaching of the Christian faith they laughed with open mouths. [[1:18|but to them that are saved|His autem qui salvi fiunt]], that is, to us, namely the elect, [[1:18|it is the power of God|virtus Dei est]], that is, a mighty effect of the divine power, through which we obtain grace and glory, and victory too against the snares of the enemy, according to the words: [[1 John 5:4|this is the victory which overcameth the world: Our faith|Hæc est victoria quæ vincit mundum, fides nostra]]: [[1 John 5:5|Who is he that overcometh the world, but he that believeth that Jesus is the Son of God|quis enim est qui vincit mundum, nisi qui credit quoniam Jesus est Filius Dei]]?

paras.t: Quod autem verbum crucis pereuntibus, scilicet prudentibus hujus sæculi, stultitia sit, probat Apostolus. Scriptum est enim in Isaia: Perdam, id est, damnabo ego Dominus Deus, sapientiam sapientium, id est sapientiam eorum qui se ipsos sapientes reputant in divinis, videlicet in naturali notitia divinorum, sicut philosophi; et prudentiam prudentium, id est falsam prudentiam impiorum, qui in rebus humanis astuti et callidi sunt ut faciant mala, reprobabo, id est, a prædicatoribus sanctis excludam, et eam in judicio condemnabo, quia non fuit subjecta simplicitati fidei sanctæ. Hinc enim ait Salvator: Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cæli et terræ, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis. Nostra translatio habet sic: Peribit sapientia a sapientibus, et intellectus prudentium abscondetur. Ubi sapiens hujus mundi, quantum ad divina naturaliter nota? ubi scriba, id est doctor moralis in lege peritus? ubi conquisitor hujus sæculi, id est investigator rerum mundanarum ac naturalium artium? Tanquam dicat: Ecce quam subito omnes isti perierunt, eo quod veram ac christianam sapientiam non receperunt. Hæc verba ex Isaia sumpta sunt, sic dicente: Ubi est litteratus? ubi verba legis ponderans? ubi doctor parvulorum? Nonne stultam fecit, id est, vanam et falsam ostendit, Deus sapientiam hujus mundi, asserendo quod illa negat, videlicet articulos fidei, et agendo quod illa impossibile reputat, utpote opera supernaturalia ad fidei confirmationem, quum tamen naturalis sapientia dicat ea non posse fieri quæ naturalem entium cursum excedunt?
paras.en: That the word of the cross is foolishness to those who perish, namely to the prudent of this world, the Apostle proves. [[1:19|For it is written|Scriptum est enim]] in Isaias[[Is 29:14||]]: [[1:19|I will destroy|Perdam]], that is, I the Lord God will condemn, [[1:19|the wisdom of the wise|sapientiam sapientium]], that is, the wisdom of those who think themselves wise in divine things, namely in the natural knowledge of divine things, like the philosophers; [[1:19|and the prudence of the prudent|et prudentiam prudentium]], that is, the false prudence of the wicked, who are astute and cunning in human affairs so as to do evil, [[1:19|I will reject|reprobabo]], that is, I will shut it out from the holy preachers and condemn it in the judgment, because it was not subject to the simplicity of the holy faith. Hence the Saviour says: [[Matt 11:25|I confess to thee, O Father, Lord of Heaven and earth, because thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to little ones|Confiteor tibi, Pater, Domine cæli et terræ, quia abscondisti hæc a sapientibus et prudentibus, et revelasti ea parvulis]]. Our translation has it thus: [[Is 29:14|wisdom shall perish from their wise men, and the understanding of their prudent men shall be hid|Peribit sapientia a sapientibus, et intellectus prudentium abscondetur]]. [[1:20|Where is the wise|Ubi sapiens]] of this world, as to divine things known by nature? [[1:20|Where is the scribe|ubi scriba]], that is, the teacher of morals skilled in the law? [[1:20|Where is the disputer of this world|ubi conquisitor hujus sæculi]], that is, the investigator of worldly things and natural arts? As if he said: see how suddenly all these have perished, because they did not receive the true and Christian wisdom. These words are taken from Isaias, who says: [[Is 33:18|where is the learned? where is he that pondered the words of the law? where is the teacher of little ones|Ubi est litteratus? ubi verba legis ponderans? ubi doctor parvulorum]]? [[1:20|Hath not God made foolish the wisdom of this world|Nonne stultam fecit Deus sapientiam hujus mundi?]]: made foolish, that is, shown to be vain and false, by asserting what it denies, namely the articles of faith, and by doing what it thinks impossible, namely supernatural works for the confirming of the faith, though natural wisdom says that what exceeds the natural course of things cannot be done?

paras.t: Nam quia in Dei sapientia, id est secundum Deum, seu divino judicio, non cognovit mundus, id est homo quilibet mundum inhabitans, per sapientiam naturalem, Deum; placuit Deo per stultitiam prædicationis, id est per prædicationem evangelicam, quam mundus fatuam reputavit, salvos facere credentes, id est electos, convertendo eos ad fidem et gratiam per Apostolorum prædicationem. Mundus utique aliquo modo cognovit Deum per sapientiam naturalem. Dictum est enim ad Romanos : Invisibilia Dei, per ea quæ facta sunt, a creatura mundi conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas. Nec dubium quin philosophi multa vera atque subtilia de divinis conscripserint. Sed quoniam ista cognitio Dei erat sine fide et opere meritorio, informis fuit, et Deo inaccepta. Idcirco, Non cognovit mundus Deum per sapientiam humanam, in sapientia Dei, id est secundum Deum seu acceptionem divinam. Propter quod ait Joannes : Qui dicit se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non custodit, mendax est. Et Salvator ad impios : Nescio, inquit, vos ; cognitionem qua dicitis mihi, Domine, Domine, non approbo. Potest quoque per sapientiam Dei intelligi æterna Sapientia incarnata : in qua mundus Deum non cognovit, quia nec eam cognovit. Propter quod Filius ait : Pater juste, mundus te non cognovit. Lux quippe in tenebris lucet, et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt.
paras.en: [[1:21|For, seeing that in the wisdom of God|Nam quia in Dei sapientia]], that is, according to God, or in the divine judgment, [[1:21|the world, by wisdom, knew not God|non cognovit mundus … per sapientiam … Deum]]: the world, that is, every man who lives in the world, did not know God by natural wisdom; [[1:21|it pleased God, by the foolishness of our preaching|placuit Deo per stultitiam prædicationis]], that is, by the preaching of the Gospel, which the world thought silly, [[1:21|to save them that believe|salvos facere credentes]], that is, the elect, converting them to faith and grace by the preaching of the Apostles. The world did indeed know God in some way by natural wisdom. For it was said to the Romans: [[Rom 1:20|the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made. His eternal power also and divinity|Invisibilia Dei, per ea quæ facta sunt, a creatura mundi conspiciuntur; sempiterna quoque virtus ejus et divinitas]]. Nor is there any doubt that the philosophers wrote many true and subtle things about divine matters. But since that knowledge of God was without faith and meritorious works, it was unformed [that is, not given life by charity], and not acceptable to God. Therefore the world did not know God by human wisdom in the wisdom of God, that is, according to God, or as God accepts it. For this reason John says: [[1 John 2:4|He who saith that he knoweth him and keepeth not his commandments is a liar|Qui dicit se nosse Deum, et mandata ejus non custodit, mendax est]]. And the Saviour says to the wicked: I know you not[[Matt 7:23||]]; I do not approve the knowledge by which you say to Me, Lord, Lord. By the wisdom of God can also be understood the eternal Wisdom incarnate: in which the world did not know God, because it did not know Wisdom either. For this reason the Son says: [[John 17:25|Just Father, the world hath not known thee|Pater juste, mundus te non cognovit]]. For [[John 1:5|the light shineth in darkness: and the darkness did not comprehend it|Lux quippe in tenebris lucet, et tenebræ eam non comprehenderunt]].

paras.t: Itaque, Non cognovit mundus per sapientiam Deum cognitione formata ac salutari. Cujus signum vel ratio est : Quoniam et Judæi signa petunt, id est, ea quæ ipsis dicuntur, per signum aliquod divinæ virtutis quærunt confirmari, ut sciant illud esse a Deo per experientiam alicujus miraculi : quod sæpe illicitum est, et ad tentationem Dei pertinet. Unicuique enim sufficere debet assertio Dei. Quoniam autem Judæi primo legem receperunt in monte Sinai cum ingenti gloria miraculorum divinorum, assueti erant petere signum quum aliquid magni dicebatur. Unde et Christo dicebant : Quod signum ostendis nobis ? Sic Abraham, Gedeon, Ezechias et alii multi Judæorum signa petierunt ; sicut et Zacharias pater Joannis. Et Græci, præsertim philosophi, et multi gentilium, sapientiam naturalem quærunt, id est, per rationes naturales et demonstrativas volunt sibi probari quod dicitur. Assueti sunt enim argumentationibus humanis insistere. Nullus ergo istorum per sapientiam suam Deum novit salubriter, quantum ad ea quæ concernunt salutem. Nos autem Apostoli prædicamus Christum crucifixum : Judæis quidem scandalum, id est confusionem et ignominiæ causam. Hoc enim ad maximam Judæorum confusionem pertinet, quod aperte docemus eos Christum in lege promissum, Dei unigenitum Filium, occidisse : quod est eis æternæ ignominiæ causa. Vel dicitur Christus Judæis scandalum, quoniam fuit eis, et adhuc est, occasio ruendi in culpam et pœnam. Nam, ut Evangelistæ testantur, sæpe scandalizabantur in eo. Propter quod dixit : Beatus est qui non fuerit scandalizatus in me. Gentibus autem, id est infidelibus, stultitiam. Nam stultum putabant quod evangelizabatur de Christo, videlicet, quod Deus æternus factus esset homo temporalis, quod impassibilis esset mortuus, immensus in utero clausus, immutabilis de novo incarnatus, quod virgo peperisset. Hæc omnia fabulosa putabant, quoniam non potuerunt videre, nec credere voluerunt, in una Persona duas perfectas esse naturas, divinam atque humanam, salvis utriusque naturalibus proprietatibus.
paras.en: So the world did not know God by wisdom with a knowledge formed [by charity] and saving. The sign or reason of this is: [[1:22|For both the Jews require signs|Quoniam et Judæi signa petunt]], that is, they seek to have what is said to them confirmed by some sign of divine power, so as to know it is from God by the experience of some miracle: which is often unlawful and amounts to tempting God. For the word of God ought to be enough for everyone. Since the Jews first received the law on Mount Sinai with an immense glory of divine miracles, they were used to asking for a sign when anything great was said. So they said to Christ too: [[John 2:18|What sign dost thou shew unto us|Quod signum ostendis nobis]]? So Abraham, Gedeon, Ezechias and many other Jews asked for signs; as did Zachary, the father of John. [[1:22|and the Greeks seek after wisdom|Et Græci … sapientiam … quærunt]]: the Greeks, especially the philosophers, and many of the Gentiles, seek natural wisdom, that is, they want what is said to be proved to them by natural and demonstrative reasons. For they are used to relying on human arguments. None of these, then, knew God by his wisdom savingly, as regards what concerns salvation. [[1:23|But we preach Christ crucified|Nos autem Apostoli prædicamus Christum crucifixum]]: we Apostles; [[1:23|unto the Jews indeed a stumblingblock|Judæis quidem scandalum]], that is, a confusion and cause of disgrace. For this belongs to the greatest confusion of the Jews, that we openly teach that they killed the Christ promised in the law, the only-begotten Son of God: which is a cause of everlasting disgrace to them. Or Christ is called a stumblingblock to the Jews because He was, and still is, an occasion of falling into guilt and punishment for them. For, as the Evangelists testify, they were often scandalized in Him. For this reason He said: [[Matt 11:6|blessed is he that shall not be scandalized in me|Beatus est qui non fuerit scandalizatus in me]]. [[1:23|and unto the Gentiles foolishness|gentibus autem stultitiam]], that is, to unbelievers. For they thought foolish what was preached of Christ, namely that the eternal God had become a man in time, that the impassible had died, the immense been enclosed in a womb, the unchangeable newly made flesh, that a virgin had given birth. All these they thought fables, because they could not see, nor would believe, that in one Person there are two perfect natures, divine and human, the natural properties of each being kept.

paras.t: Ipsis autem vocatis, id est ad fidem gratiamque electis, Judæis atque Græcis, id est gentilibus, ex quibus tanquam duobus parietibus, in Christo lapide angulari concurrentibus, constructa est sancta Ecclesia. His ergo prædicamus Christum Dei virtutem, et Dei sapientiam, id est, hoc eis affirmamus, quod Christus sit virtus ac sapientia Patris. Ipse enim est virtus et manus et brachium Patris, per quem facta sunt omnia. De quo Isaias ait : Paravit, inquit, Dominus brachium sanctum suum in oculis omnium gentium.
paras.en: [[1:24|But unto them that are called|Ipsis autem vocatis]], that is, chosen for faith and grace, [[1:24|both Jews and Greeks|Judæis atque Græcis]], that is, Gentiles, of whom, as of two walls meeting in Christ the corner stone[[Eph 2:20||]], holy Church is built. To these, then, we preach [[1:24|Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God|Christum Dei virtutem, et Dei sapientiam]], that is, we affirm to them that Christ is the power and wisdom of the Father. For He is the power and hand and arm of the Father, through whom all things were made. Of whom Isaias says: [[Is 52:10|The Lord hath prepared his holy arm in the sight of all the Gentiles|Paravit, inquit, Dominus brachium sanctum suum in oculis omnium gentium]].

paras.t: Præterea, secundum utramque naturam dicitur Christus virtus et sapientia Patris. Secundum divinam enim naturam est virtus Patris, quia per ipsum omnia facta sunt, juxta illud, Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt ; et quia potentia Patris perfecte atque plenissime relucet in Filio : in hoc namque quod Pater genuit Filium sibi consubstantialem, coæternum et coæqualem, apparet infinita potentia Patris. Dicitur quoque sapientia Patris, quum sit verbum mentis paternæ : quoniam enim ab intellectu Patris procedit, ea quæ ad intellectum pertinent, appropriata vel propria sunt Filio : ideo dicitur veritas et sapientia Patris. Et etiam, quia sapientia Patris in ipso plene relucet : est enim Filius perfecta expressio sapientiæ Patris, conceptus et dictio intellectus paterni. — Secundum humanam quoque naturam vocatur virtus et sapientia Patris, propter maximam participationem atque præcipuam relucentiam divinæ virtutis ac sapientiæ in ipso Dei et hominum mediatore. Nam ipse secundum humanam naturam passus est, et toti mundo æternam vitam promeruit, et dæmonem stravit, infernum confregit, cœlos aperuit. Sapientia vero Dei in Christi incarnatione, passione et mundi salvatione, ineffabiliter manifestatur : ut scilicet per Dei incarnationem homo deificaretur, per illius humiliationem homo exaltaretur, per illius occisionem homo vivificaretur, per illius indebitas pœnas homo a debitis pœnis solveretur, per illius caritatem homo repararetur, qui per diaboli invidiam perditus fuit. Nec potuit peccati enormitas, divinæ caritatis ardor, divinæ justitiæ magnitudo, æternæ beatitudinis dignitas, infernalis pœnæ acerbitas, humanæ naturæ nobilitas, divinæ pietatis immensitas, subtilius, evidentius aut speciosius declarari, nisi ut ipsemet Deus, Dei unigenitus Filius, hominem per suam incarnationem ac mortem redimeret. Longum esset hæc prosequi : ideo legentis contemplationi istorum pleniorem considerationem committo. Ut enim B. Thomas in Summa contra gentiles testatur, quanto homo devotus ac pius incarnationem Dei humilius et affectuosius pensat, tanto plures sibi rationes occurrunt hujus supersanctissimæ incarnationis, quæ sapientibus et prudentibus in propriis oculis abscondantur. — Postremo, sciendum quod Christus secundum neutram naturam dicitur virtus et sapientia Patris formaliter, quasi Pater non esset potens et sapiens nisi per Filium. Imo Pater in se ipso potens et sapiens est, vel potius virtus et sapientia, sicut et Spiritus Sanctus. Quomodo enim generaret Filium potentem ac sapientem, si ipse in se ipso potens non esset ac sapiens ? Quælibet ergo divina Persona, quum sit absolute perfecta, est virtus infinita, et sapientia vere immensa ; et omnes simul sunt una virtus et una sapientia absolute accepta.
paras.en: Further, Christ is called the power and wisdom of the Father according to each nature. According to the divine nature He is the power of the Father, because all things were made through Him, according to the words, [[Ps 32:6|By the word of the Lord the heavens were established|Verbo Domini cœli firmati sunt]]; and because the might of the Father shines out perfectly and most fully in the Son: for in this, that the Father begot a Son consubstantial, coeternal and coequal with Himself, the infinite might of the Father appears. He is also called the wisdom of the Father, since He is the word of the Father's mind: for since He proceeds from the Father's intellect, what belongs to the intellect is appropriated or proper to the Son: so He is called the truth[[John 14:6||]] and wisdom of the Father. And also because the wisdom of the Father shines out fully in Him: for the Son is the perfect expression of the Father's wisdom, the concept and utterance of the Father's intellect. According to the human nature too He is called the power and wisdom of the Father, because of the very great sharing and the special shining out of divine power and wisdom in Him, the mediator of God and men. For according to His human nature He suffered, and merited eternal life for the whole world, and laid low the devil, broke open hell, and opened the heavens. And the wisdom of God is unspeakably shown in Christ's incarnation, passion and the saving of the world: namely, that by God's incarnation man should be made divine, by His humiliation man be exalted, by His being slain man be given life, by His undeserved pains man be set free from deserved pains, by His charity man be restored, who had been lost [[Wis 2:24|by the envy of the devil|per diaboli invidiam]]. Nor could the enormity of sin, the ardour of divine charity, the greatness of divine justice, the dignity of eternal beatitude, the bitterness of the pains of hell, the nobility of human nature, the immensity of divine kindness, have been shown more subtly, more plainly or more beautifully, than by God Himself, the only-begotten Son of God, redeeming man by His incarnation and death. It would take long to pursue this: so I leave the fuller consideration of these things to the contemplation of the reader. For, as blessed Thomas testifies in the *Summa contra Gentiles*, the more humbly and affectionately a devout and godly man ponders the incarnation of God, the more reasons for this most holy incarnation occur to him, which are hidden from those who are wise and prudent in their own eyes. Lastly, it must be known that Christ is not called the power and wisdom of the Father formally according to either nature, as though the Father were not mighty and wise except through the Son. Rather the Father is mighty and wise in Himself, or rather is power and wisdom, as the Holy Ghost is too. For how would He beget a mighty and wise Son if He were not mighty and wise in Himself? Each divine Person, then, since it is absolutely perfect, is infinite power and truly immense wisdom; and all together are one power and one wisdom, taken absolutely.

paras.t: Quod autem in Christo reluceat virtus et sapientia Dei, declarat Apostolus. Quia quod stultum est Dei, id est quod sapientibus sæculi videtur insipienter dici de Deo, videlicet incarnari, mori et sepeliri, sapientius est hominibus, id est, magis sapientiale, seu sapientialius factum est, quam homo excogitare valeat vel intelligere ; et quod infirmum est Dei, id est, ad infirmitatem et imperfectionem Dei spectare videtur, puta laborare, fatigari, occidi, fortius est hominibus, id est efficacius ad salvandum, quam capere possit homo, omnemque humanam fortitudinem superat, quia cœlestia vincunt terrena. Efficacia namque et meritum passionis, laboris, totiusque conversationis Christi, ratione unitæ Deitatis, quodammodo infinita consistunt. Hæc autem sic se habere, patet in prædicatoribus evangelicæ legis, et in conversis per eos ad fidem. Ideo subditur : Videte, id est, diligenter perpendite, vocationem vestram activam et passivam, fratres, id est a quibus vocati estis ad fidem, et quales vos qui conversi estis, sitis ; quia non multi sapientes secundum carnem, id est secundum humanam sapientiam, non multi potentes subjectorum multitudine, seu lata dominatione, non multi nobiles carnis origine, quantum ad proximos parentes, sunt inter vos. Hoc intelligi potest, tam de prædicatoribus, quam de Corinthiis conversis. Apostoli enim et alii primi discipuli, pro majori parte illitterati, simplices, pauperesque fuerunt. Tales enim elegit Deus in prædicatores et Apostolos, ne promulgatio fidei adscriberetur humanæ astutiæ atque potentiæ. Et ne attribueretur omnino simplicitati et ignorantiæ, voluit Deus quosdam paucos habere prædicatores litteratos, potentes ac nobiles: quales fuerunt Paulus iste, Nathanael, Manahen, Barnabas, etc. Et similiter illi qui primo conversi fuerunt, pro magna parte simplices, ignobiles et impotentes fuerunt.
paras.en: That the power and wisdom of God shine out in Christ, the Apostle declares. [[1:25|For the foolishness of God|Quia quod stultum est Dei]], that is, what the wise of the world think is foolishly said of God, namely that He was made flesh, died and was buried, [[1:25|is wiser than men|sapientius est hominibus]], that is, is wiser, or was done more wisely, than man can devise or understand; [[1:25|and the weakness of God|et quod infirmum est Dei]], that is, what seems to belong to weakness and imperfection in God, such as to labour, to be wearied, to be slain, [[1:25|is stronger than men|fortius est hominibus]], that is, more effective for saving than man can grasp, and surpasses all human strength, because heavenly things overcome earthly. For the efficacy and merit of the passion, the labour and the whole life of Christ are in a way infinite, by reason of the Godhead united to Him. That this is so is plain in the preachers of the law of the Gospel, and in those converted by them to the faith. So it is added: [[1:26|For see your vocation, brethren|Videte … vocationem vestram … fratres]]: see, that is, weigh carefully, your calling, active and passive, that is, by whom you were called to the faith, and what sort of men you are who have been converted; [[1:26|that there are not many wise according to the flesh|quia non multi sapientes secundum carnem]], that is, according to human wisdom, [[1:26|not many mighty|non multi potentes]] in the number of their subjects or in wide dominion, [[1:26|not many noble|non multi nobiles]] by birth in the flesh, as regards their near forebears, among you. This can be understood both of the preachers and of the converted Corinthians. For the Apostles and the other first disciples were for the most part unlettered[[Acts 4:13||]], simple and poor. For God chose such men as preachers and Apostles, lest the spreading of the faith be ascribed to human cunning and power. And lest it be ascribed wholly to simplicity and ignorance, God willed to have a few preachers who were learned, mighty and noble: such as this Paul, Nathanael, Manahen, Barnabas, etc. And likewise those who were first converted were for the most part simple, of low birth and without power.

paras.t: Sed quæ stulta sunt mundi, id est illitteratos, quos mundus stultos putavit, elegit Deus, scilicet Apostolos et alios plures, ut confundat sapientes sæculi hujus, id est, eos vere insipientes ostendat, abscondendo eis divina mysteria. Per Apostolos quoque victa, in nihilumque redacta est horum vana sapientia, sicut et prædixit: Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri. Et infirma mundi, id est homines impotentes, elegit Deus, ut confundat fortia, id est potentes, dum isti impotentes per humilitatem salvantur, potentes vero cum sua præsumptione damnantur. Et ignobilia mundi et contemptibilia, id est homines ignobiles, a mundo contemptos, elegit Deus ab æterno, id est, tales prædestinavit ad vitam, et ea quæ non sunt, id est, qui nihil reputabantur, ut ea quæ sunt destrueret, id est, illos qui magni habentur in mundo et aliquid esse se putant, humiliaret, præferendo eis abjectos et inopes. Ut non glorietur omnis caro in conspectu ejus, id est, ne aliquis homo glorietur inaniter in conspectu divino, aliquid boni adscribendo sibimetipsi, quasi sua sapientia, potentia seu nobilitate salvatus sit.
paras.en: [[1:27|But the foolish things of the world hath God chosen|sed quæ stulta sunt mundi elegit Deus]]: the foolish things, that is, the unlettered, whom the world thought foolish, namely the Apostles and many others, [[1:27|that he may confound the wise|ut confundat sapientes]] of this world, that is, show them to be truly foolish, by hiding the divine mysteries from them. Through the Apostles too their vain wisdom was overcome and brought to nothing, as He foretold: [[Luke 21:15|I will give you a mouth and wisdom, which all your adversaries shall not be able to resist and gainsay|Ego dabo vobis os et sapientiam, cui non poterunt resistere et contradicere omnes adversarii vestri]]. [[1:27|and the weak things of the world hath God chosen|et infirma mundi elegit Deus]], that is, men without power, [[1:27|that he may confound the strong|ut confundat fortia]], that is, the mighty, while those without power are saved by humility, and the mighty are damned with their presumption. [[1:28|And the base things of the world and the things that are contemptible, hath God chosen|et ignobilia mundi, et contemptibilia elegit Deus]], that is, men of low birth, despised by the world, God has chosen from eternity, that is, has predestined such to life, [[1:28|and things that are not|et ea quæ non sunt]], that is, those who were counted nothing, [[1:28|that he might bring to nought things that are|ut ea quæ sunt destrueret]], that is, that He might humble those who are held great in the world and think themselves to be something, by preferring the outcast and needy to them. [[1:29|That no flesh should glory in his sight|Ut non glorietur omnis caro in conspectu ejus]], that is, lest any man glory vainly in the sight of God, ascribing some good to himself, as if he had been saved by his own wisdom, power or nobility.

paras.t: Ex ipso autem, id est dono et gratia Dei, vos estis per fidem et opera bona, in Christo Jesu capite nostro, qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo, id est, datus et missus est nobis a Patre, ut nos illuminaret. Ipse enim est lux illuminans omnem hominem. De quo scriptum est: Tempus requirendi Dominum, quum venerit qui docebit vos justitiam; et alibi, Exsultate in Domino, quia dedit vobis doctorem justitiæ. Ad Christum quoque Pater ait per Isaiam: Dedi te in lucem gentium. Factus est nobis quoque Christus justitia, id est causa justitiæ, satisfaciendo pro nobis per viam justitiæ, et suo merito nos justificans. Propter quod et dictum est Romanis: Sicut per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur multi. Et sanctificatio, quoniam in Baptismo mundavit nos ab omni inquinamento, deinde in Pœnitentiæ sacramento; et redemptio, quia patiendo pro nobis, redemit nos. Totum igitur bonum est, dependet ac fluit a Christo, ut quemadmodum scriptum est per Jeremiam prophetam, Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur, non in se ipso; nec in aliquo bono sibi concesso, ibi sistendo, nec in rebus caducis vane exsultet, sed solum in Domino, laudando, regratiando, contemplando, diligendo, et bene vivendo. Sic enim in Jeremia legitur: Non glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua, et non glorietur fortis in fortitudine sua, et non glorietur dives in divitiis suis; sed in hoc glorietur qui gloriatur, scire et nosse me. Sic gloriabatur Virgo Christifera: Exsultavit, inquiens, spiritus meus in Deo salutari meo. Et Habacuc propheta: Ego autem in Domino gaudebo, et exsultabo in Deo salutari meo.
paras.en: [[1:30|But of him are you|Ex ipso autem vos estis]]: of Him, that is, by the gift and grace of God, you are, through faith and good works, [[1:30|in Christ Jesus|in Christo Jesu]] our head, [[1:30|who of God is made unto us wisdom|qui factus est nobis sapientia a Deo]], that is, was given and sent to us by the Father to enlighten us. For He is [[John 1:9|the true light, which enlighteneth every man|lux illuminans omnem hominem]]. Of whom it is written: [[Osee 10:12|the time to seek the Lord is, when he shall come that shall teach you justice|Tempus requirendi Dominum, quum venerit qui docebit vos justitiam]]; and elsewhere, [[Joel 2:23|rejoice, and be joyful in the Lord your God: because he hath given you a teacher of justice|Exsultate in Domino, quia dedit vobis doctorem justitiæ]]. And the Father says to Christ through Isaias: [[Is 49:6|I have given thee to be the light of the Gentiles|Dedi te in lucem gentium]]. Christ has also been made for us [[1:30|justice|justitia]], that is, the cause of justice, by making satisfaction for us by way of justice, and justifying us by His merit. For this reason it was said to the Romans: [[Rom 5:19|as by the disobedience of one man, many were made sinners: so also by the obedience of one, many shall be made just|Sicut per unius inobedientiam peccatores constituti sunt multi, ita per unius obedientiam justi constituentur multi]]. [[1:30|and sanctification|Et sanctificatio]], because in Baptism He cleansed us from all defilement, and then in the sacrament of Penance; [[1:30|and redemption|et redemptio]], because by suffering for us He redeemed us. All good, then, depends on and flows from Christ, [[1:31|That, as it is written|ut quemadmodum scriptum est]] through the prophet Jeremias, [[1:31|He that glorieth may glory in the Lord|Qui gloriatur, in Domino glorietur]], not in himself; nor in any good granted him, stopping there; nor let him exult vainly in perishing things, but only in the Lord, by praising, thanking, contemplating, loving and living well. For so we read in Jeremias: [[Jer 9:23|Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, and let not the strong man glory in his strength, and let not the rich man glory in his riches|Non glorietur sapiens in sapientia sua, et non glorietur fortis in fortitudine sua, et non glorietur dives in divitiis suis]]; [[Jer 9:24|But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me|sed in hoc glorietur qui gloriatur, scire et nosse me]]. So the Virgin who bore Christ gloried, saying: [[Luke 1:47|my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour|Exsultavit, inquiens, spiritus meus in Deo salutari meo]]. And the prophet Habacuc: [[Hab 3:18|But I will rejoice in the Lord: and I will joy in God my Jesus|Ego autem in Domino gaudebo, et exsultabo in Deo salutari meo]] [Denis has *salutari meo*, "my Saviour", for the Vulgate's *Jesu meo*].

3.title: Elucidatio capituli tertii: Et ego, fratres, non potui vobis loqui
3.title_en: Explanation of the third chapter: And I, brethren, could not speak to you

paras.t: Adhuc autem Apostolus clarius prosequitur imperfectionem Corinthiorum, et causam contentionis eorum aufert ; et ait : Et ego, fratres, non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus : id est, alta mysteria fidei et sublimia de divinitate Christi, perfecta quoque internæ perfectionis exercitia, non potui vobis proponere, sed parva et rudia atque humilia de Christi humanitate vobis proposui, non judicans me aliquid scire inter vos, nisi Jesum, et hunc crucifixum. Tanquam parvulis, id est imperfectis, in Christo, lac, id est facilem doctrinam et teneram instructionem, vobis potum dedi, id est, tali doctrina spiritualiter vos potavi, et animas vestras rigavi, non escam, id est, non solidum cibum, non profundam sapientiam, non sublimem vitæ perfectionem vobis tradere potui. Nondum enim poteratis spiritualiter capere talia ; sed nec nunc quidem potestis : adhuc enim carnales estis, id est carnalibus vitiis subjacentes. Quum enim sit inter vos zelus, id est invidia latens, et contentio, id est lis verborum inde procedens, nonne carnales estis (pro eodem sumit Apostolus carnalem et animalem), et secundum hominem ambulatis, id est, secundum humanam fragilitatem, imperfectionem et ignorantiam vivitis et sentitis? Quum enim quis, id est aliquis vestrum, dicat, Ego quidem sum Pauli, alius autem, Ego Apollo, id est, unus dicit se baptizatum a Paulo, alius ab Apolline, et idcirco unus se alteri præfert, nonne homines estis? id est, vitia hominibus consueta sectamini, et non estis divini, sed homines nudi, humanum sensum sequentes, non Spiritus Sancti instinctum.
paras.en: The Apostle goes on still more plainly about the imperfection of the Corinthians, and takes away the cause of their contention; and he says: [[3:1|And I, brethren, could not speak to you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal|Et ego, fratres, non potui vobis loqui quasi spiritualibus, sed quasi carnalibus]]: that is, I could not set before you the high mysteries of the faith and sublime things about the divinity of Christ, nor the perfect exercises of inward perfection, but I set before you small, simple and lowly things about the humanity of Christ, [[1 Cor 2:2|For I judged not myself to know anything among you, but Jesus Christ: and him crucified|non judicans me aliquid scire inter vos, nisi Jesum, et hunc crucifixum]]. [[3:1|As unto little ones|Tanquam parvulis]], that is, the imperfect, [[3:1|in Christ|in Christo]], [[3:2|I gave you milk to drink|lac vobis potum dedi]]: milk, that is, easy teaching and tender instruction; I gave you to drink, that is, I gave you such teaching to drink spiritually and watered your souls; [[3:2|not meat|non escam]], that is, I could not give you solid food[[Heb 5:14||]], deep wisdom, sublime perfection of life. [[3:2|for you were not able as yet|Nondum enim poteratis]] to take such things in spiritually; [[3:2|But neither indeed are you now able: for you are yet carnal|sed nec nunc quidem potestis : adhuc enim carnales estis]], that is, subject to carnal vices.
